title: NASA GISS Global Temperature Anomaly
text:
Load Data


Code
library(highcharter)

df_nasa <- read.csv(
  "https://data.giss.nasa.gov/gistemp/tabledata_v4/GLB.Ts+dSST.csv",
  header = TRUE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, na.strings = "***", skip = 1
)

dfm <- df_nasa <- df_nasa[, c("Year", "Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun",
                               "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec")]

dfma <- data.frame(
  Year   = df_nasa$Year,
  lower  = apply(dfm[, 2:length(dfm)], 1, min, na.rm = TRUE),
  upper  = apply(dfm[, 2:length(dfm)], 1, max, na.rm = TRUE),
  decade = paste0(substr(df_nasa$Year, 1, 3), 0)
)

dfr     <- reshape::melt(df_nasa, id.vars = "Year", variable_name = "month")
df_nasa <- merge(dfr, dfma, sort = FALSE)
df_nasa$month <- as.character(df_nasa$month)
df_nasa$year_mon <- paste0(
  df_nasa$Year, "-",
  stringr::str_pad(
    sapply(df_nasa$month, function(x) grep(paste("(?i)", x, sep = ""), month.abb)),
    2, pad = "0"
  ),
  "-01"
)
names(df_nasa) <- tolower(names(df_nasa))
df_nasa <- df_nasa[, c("year_mon", "value", "lower", "upper", "year", "decade", "month")]
df_nasa$decade <- as.numeric(df_nasa$decade)
df <- df_nasa[order(df_nasa$year_mon), ]

caption_text <- "Temperature deviation (°C) from the 1951–1980 baseline, combining land surface and ocean measurements (1880–2026). Negative values indicate cooler periods; positive values indicate warming. Recent years (2023–2024) exceed +1.2°C, approaching the Paris Agreement 1.5°C threshold. Source: NASA GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (GISTEMP v4)."

  dplyr::group_by(year) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(value = median(value)) %>%
  dplyr::ungroup() %>%

  dplyr::do(data = .$value, color = dplyr::first(.$color_y)) %>%

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
text:
Between 2010 and 2013 six euro countries ran into deep trouble: Greece, Ireland, Portugal, Spain, Cyprus and Italy. Five of them needed rescue loans from the other euro countries, and all six went through years of cuts and lost jobs. They started from the same crisis, but they did not end up in the same place: in 2024 the average person in Ireland produced almost twice as much as in 2008, while in Greece it was still less than in 2008.
This data story compares the six countries, in plain words, on:

borrowing — how much more each country bought from abroad than it sold, before the crisis,
income — how much the country produces per person,
jobs — how many people who want work cannot find it,
investment — what the country spends on its future,
exports — how much it sells to the rest of the world,
people — whether its population grew or shrank.

Greece is in red throughout and the other five in gray. It follows on from Greece Since 2000, which tells the Greek story on its own. All the data comes from golemworldbank, an R package and Shiny app for exploring World Bank indicators; the page carries its own copy of the data for these six countries and of the one function it uses, so it runs without installing anything from GitHub.

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
text:
The data
golemworldbank ships the World Bank’s World Development Indicators as one long table, mfi: one row per country, indicator and year. R/mfi_euro_crisis.rds holds its rows for the six countries from 2000 onwards, every indicator. We keep the indicators this story needs, each with a short name:


Code
# golemworldbank's mfi, six countries from 2000 (with the package installed, its mfi has every country)
mfi <- readRDS(paste0(directory, "R/mfi_euro_crisis.rds"))

countries <- c("Greece", "Ireland", "Portugal", "Spain", "Cyprus", "Italy")
last_year <- 2024   # the latest year with complete numbers: 2025 is still incomplete
indicators <- c(
  income             = "GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$)",
  income_gni         = "GNI per capita (constant 2015 US$)",
  unemployment       = "Unemployment, total (% of total labor force) (modeled ILO estimate)",
  youth_unemployment = "Unemployment, youth total (% of total labor force ages 15-24) (modeled ILO estimate)",
  investment         = "Gross fixed capital formation (% of GDP)",
  current_account    = "Current account balance (% of GDP)",
  exports            = "Exports of goods and services (% of GDP)",
  population         = "Population, total"
)

df_peers <- mfi %>%
  filter(`Country Name` %in% countries, `Indicator Name` %in% indicators) %>%
  mutate(country = `Country Name`,
         year    = as.numeric(as.character(Year)),
         measure = names(indicators)[match(`Indicator Name`, indicators)]) %>%
  select(country, measure, year, value) %>%
  arrange(country, measure, year)

Each row is one country, one indicator, one year:







Column
Description

The World Bank’s value for that country and year



A few of these need a word of explanation:

Income (GDP per person) is the value of everything a country produces in a year, divided by the number of people who live there, in US dollars with price rises removed, so that years can be compared fairly. It is a rough measure of how well off the average person is.
Borrowing from abroad (the current account) is what a country earns from the rest of the world minus what it pays to it, as a share of everything it produces. A minus means it bought more than it sold and borrowed to pay the difference.
Investment is the money spent on things that help a country earn more later: new buildings, factories, machines, roads and equipment, as a share of everything the economy produces.

Every chart shades the euro crisis (2008 to 2013) and COVID (2020), and writes each country’s latest value at the end of its line; labels that would overlap are moved apart and joined to their line:


Code
# a measure's value for one country and year, and the change between two values
at <- function(m, cty, y) df_peers$value[df_peers$measure == m & df_peers$country == cty & df_peers$year == y]
change_pct <- function(from, to) round((to - from) / from * 100)
big <- function(v) format(round(v), big.mark = ",")

# Greece in red, the others in gray (as in the Greek Wages and Housing races)
highlight <- "Greece"
colour_of <- function(cty) ifelse(cty == highlight, "#E74C3C", "#B3B3B3")

shocks <- list(list(from = 2008,   to = 2013,   label = "Euro crisis"),
               list(from = 2019.5, to = 2020.5, label = "COVID"))

# chart height in pixels, set on the widget itself (width stays 100% of the
# page), so the chart always fills the box it is drawn in — no scroll bars.
# Returned inside a tagList: printed straight from a chunk, a widget's height
# is overridden by the chunk's figure size; inside a tagList it is kept
# The plotly toolbar goes down the right edge, so it never covers a long title
sized <- function(p, h) {
  p <- plotly::layout(p, modebar = list(orientation = "v"))
  p$height <- h
  htmltools::tagList(p)
}

# data source as a footnote inside each chart, at the bottom of the bottom
# margin `b` (in pixels), so it lands in the same place whatever the height
source_note <- function(b) {
  list(text = "Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators, via <a href='https://github.com/sedzinfo/golemworldbank'>golemworldbank</a>",
       xref = "paper", yref = "paper", x = 1, y = 0, yshift = -(b - 22),
       xanchor = "right", yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE,
       font = list(size = 11, color = "gray50"))
}

# end labels: each sits right of its line's last point; labels closer than
# `gap` pixels are pushed upwards and joined to their point by a leader line.
# `per_px` is how many y units one pixel of the plot is worth
end_labels <- function(ends, per_px, unit, gap = 17) {
  o <- order(ends$value)
  y <- ends$value[o]
  for (i in seq_along(y)[-1]) y[i] <- max(y[i], y[i - 1] + gap * per_px)
  ends$label_y[o] <- y
  lapply(seq_len(nrow(ends)), function(i) {
    name <- if (ends$country[i] == highlight) paste0("<b>", ends$country[i], "</b>") else ends$country[i]
    list(x = ends$year[i], y = ends$value[i], xref = "x", yref = "y",
         ax = 24, ay = -(ends$label_y[i] - ends$value[i]) / per_px,
         showarrow = TRUE, arrowhead = 0, arrowwidth = 1, arrowcolor = "#B3B3B3",
         xanchor = "left", text = paste0(name, " ", ends$text[i]),
         font = list(size = 12, color = "gray25"))
  })
}

# one line per country, Greece drawn last so it sits on top. `index_year`
# turns each line into "that year = 100"; `ref` draws a dotted reference line
peer_chart <- function(m, title, ytitle, unit = "", index_year = NULL, ref = NULL,
                       tozero = TRUE, h = 520) {
  d <- df_peers[df_peers$measure == m & df_peers$year >= 2000 & df_peers$year <= last_year, ]
  if (!is.null(index_year)) {
    d <- d %>% group_by(country) %>%
      mutate(value = value / value[year == index_year] * 100) %>% ungroup()
  }
  fmt <- function(v) if (unit == "$") paste0("$", big(v)) else paste0(round(v, 1), unit)
  p <- plot_ly()
  for (cty in c(setdiff(countries, highlight), highlight)) {
    dc <- d[d$country == cty, ]
    p <- add_lines(p, data = dc, x = ~year, y = ~value, name = cty,
                   line = list(color = colour_of(cty), width = if (cty == highlight) 3 else 2),
                   text = paste0(cty, " · ", dc$year, "<br>", fmt(dc$value)), hoverinfo = "text")
  }
  ends <- d %>% filter(!is.na(value)) %>% group_by(country) %>% slice_max(year) %>% ungroup() %>%
    mutate(text = fmt(value))
  b <- 110
  lo <- if (tozero) min(0, d$value, na.rm = TRUE) else min(d$value, na.rm = TRUE)
  per_px <- (max(d$value, na.rm = TRUE) - lo) * 1.1 / (h - 90 - b)
  shapes <- lapply(shocks, function(s) {
    list(type = "rect", xref = "x", yref = "paper", x0 = s$from, x1 = s$to, y0 = 0, y1 = 1,
         fillcolor = "gray92", line = list(width = 0), layer = "below")
  })
  if (!is.null(ref)) {
    shapes <- c(shapes, list(list(type = "line", xref = "paper", x0 = 0, x1 = 1, y0 = ref, y1 = ref,
                                  line = list(dash = "dot", color = "gray"))))
  }
  tags <- lapply(shocks, function(s) {
    list(x = (s$from + s$to) / 2, y = 1, xref = "x", yref = "paper", yanchor = "bottom",
         text = s$label, showarrow = FALSE, font = list(size = 12, color = "gray40"))
  })
  plotly::layout(p,
    title  = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    margin = list(t = 90, r = 150, b = b),
    xaxis  = list(title = "", tickangle = -90, range = c(1999.5, max(d$year) + 0.5)),
    yaxis  = list(title = ytitle, ticksuffix = if (unit == "%") "%" else "",
                  rangemode = if (tozero) "tozero" else "normal"),
    showlegend = FALSE,
    shapes = shapes,
    annotations = c(tags, end_labels(ends, per_px, unit), list(source_note(b))),
    font   = list(size = 13, color = "gray25")) %>%
    sized(h)
}

# one bar per country, largest at the top, Greece in red; a negative bar
# carries its value inside, where it cannot run into the country names
ranked_bars <- function(values, title, h = 380) {
  d <- data.frame(country = names(values), value = unname(values))
  d <- d[order(d$value), ]
  b <- 80
  plot_ly(d, x = ~value, y = ~factor(country, levels = country), type = "bar", orientation = "h",
          marker = list(color = colour_of(d$country)),
          # rounding first (+ 0 turns -0 into 0) so -0.3 reads "+0%", never "-0%"
          text = sprintf("%+.0f%%", round(d$value) + 0),
          textposition = ifelse(d$value < 0, "inside", "outside"),
          textfont = list(color = ifelse(d$value < 0, "white", "gray25")), cliponaxis = FALSE,
          hovertext = paste0(d$country, ": ", sprintf("%+.1f%%", d$value)), hoverinfo = "text") %>%
    plotly::layout(
      title  = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.95, yanchor = "top"),
      margin = list(t = 70, r = 60, b = b, l = 90),
      xaxis  = list(title = "", ticksuffix = "%", zeroline = TRUE, zerolinecolor = "gray"),
      yaxis  = list(title = ""),
      annotations = list(source_note(b)),
      font   = list(size = 13, color = "gray25")) %>%
    sized(h)
}

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
section: Before the crisis: living on borrowed money
text:
Before the crisis: living on borrowed money


Code
peer_chart("current_account",
           title  = "Buying more from abroad than selling (-) or less (+), % of the economy",
           ytitle = "% of the economy", unit = "%", ref = 0, tozero = FALSE)






In the 2000s borrowing was cheap across the euro area, and for years Greece, Portugal, Spain and Cyprus bought far more from the rest of the world than they sold, borrowing the difference. In 2008 the gap was -14.6% of everything Greece produced, -14.4% in Cyprus and -11.9% in Portugal. When the 2008 financial crisis made lenders nervous, the money stopped coming, and each country had to close the gap fast. By 2013 every one of them was close to zero. Italy borrowed little from abroad and Ireland less than the others: their problems came from a government that already owed a lot (Italy) and from banks that had lent too much on houses (Ireland).
Five of the six then needed rescue loans from the other euro countries, the International Monetary Fund or both, and in return had to cut spending and raise taxes:

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
section: Income: from almost double to still below
text:
Income: from almost double to still below
To compare countries of different sizes, each line starts at 100 in 2008: 110 means 10% more than in 2008, 90 means 10% less.


Code
peer_chart("income", index_year = 2008, ref = 100, tozero = FALSE,
           title  = "Income per person, 2008 = 100 (price rises removed)",
           ytitle = "2008 = 100")








Code
income_change <- sapply(countries, function(cty) change_pct(at("income", cty, 2008), at("income", cty, 2024)))
ranked_bars(income_change, "Income per person: change from 2008 to 2024 (%)")






All six fell into the crisis, but they came out of it at very different speeds. By 2024 income per person was +91% in Ireland against 2008, +19% in Cyprus, +13% in Portugal, +8% in Spain and +3% in Italy. Greece is the only one still below 2008, at -10%: its fall was the deepest and its rescue the longest.

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
section: Ireland’s numbers need a second look
text:
Ireland’s numbers need a second look
Ireland’s line shoots up from 2015 because of how GDP is counted. GDP includes everything produced in the country, and many large international companies have made Ireland the base of their business for tax reasons, so their profits count as Irish production. Much of that money goes back to the companies’ owners abroad. GNI subtracts it and counts only the income that stays with people in Ireland:


Code
d <- df_peers %>%
  filter(country == "Ireland", measure %in% c("income", "income_gni"), year <= last_year, !is.na(value)) %>%
  mutate(what = ifelse(measure == "income", "GDP per person (everything produced)", "GNI per person (income that stays)"))

p <- plot_ly(d, x = ~year, y = ~value, color = ~what, colors = c("#0082c8", "#E74C3C"),
             type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers", marker = list(size = 7),
             text = ~paste0("Ireland · ", year, "<br>", what, ": $", big(value)), hoverinfo = "text") %>%
  plotly::layout(title  = list(text = "Ireland: what is produced and what stays (US$ per person, price rises removed)",
                               x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
                 margin = list(t = 80, b = 150),
                 xaxis  = list(title = "", tickangle = -90),
                 yaxis  = list(title = "US$ per person", rangemode = "tozero"),
                 legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.2),
                 annotations = list(source_note(150)),
                 font   = list(size = 13, color = "gray25"))
sized(p, 520)






In 2024 Ireland’s GDP per person was $94,475, but its GNI per person $67,024. Even GNI is lifted by these companies, which is why Ireland’s own statistics office publishes a third measure that removes them; the World Bank does not carry it. The same companies explain the strange jumps in Ireland’s investment and borrowing lines below, such as investment of 53% of the economy in 2019, the year some of them moved patents and other intangible assets to Ireland. Ireland did recover strongly — its unemployment is among the lowest of the six — but by less than its GDP suggests.

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
text:
Jobs: the deepest wound
The unemployment rate counts people who want a job and are looking for one, but cannot find one.


Code
peer_chart("unemployment", unit = "%",
           title  = "People looking for work who cannot find it (%)",
           ytitle = "% of people looking for work")






In 2013, 28% of people looking for work in Greece and 26% in Spain could not find a job — more than 1 in 4. Among young people (15 to 24) it was 58% in Greece and 55% in Spain, more than half. Unemployment has fallen everywhere since, but not to the same level: by 2024 it was 4.3% in Ireland and 4.9% in Cyprus, against 10% in Greece and 11.4% in Spain.

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
text:
Investment: Greece stopped building


Code
peer_chart("investment", unit = "%",
           title  = "Investment in buildings, machines and roads (% of the economy)",
           ytitle = "% of the economy")






Investment fell in every country during the crisis. Most of them went back to around a fifth of what they produce, but Greece fell furthest — from 23% in 2008 to 12% in 2013 — and stayed there until 2019. In 2024 it was still 16%, the lowest of the six. A country that invests little for a decade has fewer new factories, machines and roads to earn from, which is one reason Greek incomes have been slowest to recover. (Ireland’s line jumps around for the reasons in the section above.)

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
text:
Exports: everyone sells more abroad


Code
peer_chart("exports", unit = "%",
           title  = "Exports of goods and services (% of the economy)",
           ytitle = "% of the economy")








Code
exports_change <- sapply(countries, function(cty) round(at("exports", cty, 2024) - at("exports", cty, 2008)))
ranked_bars(exports_change, "Exports: change from 2008 to 2024 (percentage points of the economy)")






The one thing all six did after the crisis was to sell more to the rest of the world. Greek exports went from 23% of the economy in 2008 to 42% in 2024, Portugal’s from 31% to 46%. The bar chart shows the change in percentage points: Greece’s exports grew by 19 points of its economy. Ireland’s exports are bigger than its whole economy, and Cyprus’s almost as big, because exports count the full value of what is sold, including parts that were imported first.

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
section: People: who stayed and who left
text:
People: who stayed and who left


Code
population_change <- sapply(countries, function(cty) change_pct(at("population", cty, 2008), at("population", cty, 2024)))
ranked_bars(population_change, "Population: change from 2008 to 2024 (%)")






During the crisis many people, often young and well educated, left to find work elsewhere. In the countries that recovered quickly, people came back and newcomers arrived: from 2008 to 2024 the population grew by 24% in Cyprus and 20% in Ireland. Greece’s shrank by 6%, also because Greek families have few children; Italy’s stayed about the same.

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
text:
Comparing 2008 with 2024 with indicator_change()
golemworldbank’s indicator_change() compares every indicator a country has in two years — the same comparison as the app’s Change (%) tab. Running it for each country from 2008 to 2024 and keeping the indicators of this story gives one table of percentage changes:


Code
change_2008_2024 <- bind_rows(lapply(countries, function(cty) {
  res <- indicator_change(mfi, country = cty, year1 = 2008, year2 = 2024)
  both <- rbind(res$increased, res$decreased)
  both <- both[both$Indicator %in% indicators[names(indicators) != "current_account"], ]
  data.frame(measure = names(indicators)[match(both$Indicator, indicators)],
             country = cty, change = round(both$`Change %`))
}))

change_2008_2024 %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = country, values_from = change) %>%
  arrange(match(measure, names(indicators))) %>%
  as.data.frame()

Each number is the percentage change from 2008 to 2024: income -10 for Greece means 10% less than in 2008. Unemployment, investment and exports are themselves percentages, so their change is relative to the 2008 level (unemployment in Ireland going from 6.8% to 4.3% is a change of -37%). Borrowing from abroad is left out: it is a number that can be below zero, and a percentage change of a negative number, or of one that turns from a minus into a plus, has no clear meaning.

The same start: before 2008, Greece, Cyprus, Portugal and Spain bought far more from abroad than they sold and borrowed the difference. When the borrowing stopped, all of them had to cut back at once.

Jobs came back everywhere, but Greece and Spain still have the highest unemployment of the six: 10% and 11.4% in 2024, against 4.3% to 6.5% in the other four.
Investment is where Greece differs most: it has invested the least of the six every year since 2010.
Exports grew in all six — the one recipe every country followed.
People voted with their feet: the countries that recovered fastest gained population, Greece lost it.

title: Recreating Hans Rosling’s Bubble Chart in R
section: Building the chart step by step
text:
Building the chart step by step

Step 1 — the basic scatter
Start with a single year to get the layout right before adding animation.


Code
gapminder_2007 <- gapminder[gapminder$year == 2007, ]

ggplot(gapminder_2007,
       aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, size = pop, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(title = "2007", x = "GDP per capita", y = "Life expectancy") +
  theme_minimal()









Three things are already encoded: wealth (x), health (y), and population (bubble size). Continent gets color.


Step 2 — improve the axes
GDP per capita spans from ~$200 to ~$100,000. A log scale is essential — on a linear scale, poor countries are crushed into the left margin and you lose all the variation that matters.


Code
ggplot(gapminder_2007,
       aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, size = pop, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75) +
  scale_x_log10(
    breaks = c(500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000, 50000),
    labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())
  ) +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 24), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "2007", x = "GDP per capita (log scale)", y = "Life expectancy") +
  theme_minimal()









range = c(2, 24) in scale_size maps the smallest population to a 2px bubble and the largest (China, India) to 24px. The guide = "none" removes the size legend — it’s not readable anyway.


Step 3 — label the big ones


Code
big_countries <- c("China", "India", "United States", "Brazil", "Nigeria")

ggplot(gapminder_2007,
       aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, size = pop, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_text(
    data = \(d) d[d$country %in% big_countries, ],
    aes(label = country),
    size = 3.2, vjust = -1.1, show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(
    breaks = c(500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000, 50000),
    labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())
  ) +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 24), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "2007", x = "GDP per capita (log scale)", y = "Life expectancy") +
  theme_minimal()











Step 4 — dark theme + colors


Code
continent_colors <- c(
  Africa   = "#E74C3C",
  Americas = "#F39C12",
  Asia     = "#3498DB",
  Europe   = "#2ECC71",
  Oceania  = "#9B59B6"
)

dark_theme <- theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "#0F1923", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#0F1923", color = NA),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#1E2D3D"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    text             = element_text(color = "white"),
    axis.text        = element_text(color = "#90A4AE"),
    legend.position  = "bottom",
    legend.text      = element_text(size = 11),
    plot.caption     = element_text(color = "#546E7A", size = 8, hjust = 1)
  )

ggplot(gapminder_2007,
       aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, size = pop, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75, stroke = 0.2) +
  geom_text(
    data = \(d) d[d$country %in% big_countries, ],
    aes(label = country),
    size = 3.2, vjust = -1.1, show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(
    breaks = c(500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000, 50000),
    labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())
  ) +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 24), guide = "none") +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = continent_colors,
    guide  = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 5))
  ) +
  labs(
    title   = "2007",
    x       = "GDP per capita (log scale)",
    y       = "Life expectancy at birth",
    color   = NULL,
    caption = "Source: Gapminder  |  Bubble size = population"
  ) +
  dark_theme











Step 5 — animate it
gganimate extends ggplot2 with transition_* functions. transition_time(year) moves through the year variable. shadow_mark() leaves a faint ghost trail so you can see where countries have been.


Code
p <- ggplot(gapminder,
            aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, size = pop, color = continent)) +

  geom_point(alpha = 0.75, stroke = 0.2) +

  geom_text(
    data = \(d) d[d$country %in% big_countries, ],
    aes(label = country),
    size = 3.2, vjust = -1.1, show.legend = FALSE
  ) +

  scale_x_log10(
    breaks = c(500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000, 50000),
    labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())
  ) +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 24), guide = "none") +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = continent_colors,
    guide  = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 5))
  ) +

  labs(
    title   = "{as.integer(frame_time)}",   # <-- the magic: year as title
    x       = "GDP per capita (log scale)",
    y       = "Life expectancy at birth",
    color   = NULL,
    caption = "Source: Gapminder  |  Bubble size = population"
  ) +

  dark_theme +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 54, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5)) +

  transition_time(year) +      # animate over year
  ease_aes("linear") +         # constant speed between frames
  shadow_mark(alpha = 0.06, size = 0.4)   # ghost trail

animate(p,
        nframes  = 120,
        fps      = 12,
        width    = 900,
        height   = 650,
        units    = "px",
        res      = 96,
        renderer = gifski_renderer("gapminder.gif"))










Note: rendering takes ~1–2 minutes. The GIF will appear in your working directory (getwd()).

title: Greek Housing Race: Rents, House Prices and Affordability in Europe
text:
The OECD publishes yearly analytical house price indicators for its members and partner countries: an index of rent prices, an index of house prices, and two affordability ratios — price-to-income and price-to-rent. The OECD gives them as indices with 2015 = 100; here every value is turned into a plain percentage change since 2015 — “+13%” means rents are 13% higher than in 2015. They show how much each market moved, not the level of rents in euros.
This vignette pulls the series straight from the OECD data API and builds the same kind of visualisations as the EU Salary Race: four ranked “bar chart races” (one per indicator) and a shareable GIF of each — with Greece highlighted in red against the rest of Europe in gray. It starts with a look at Greece on its own, since rents and house prices there have taken very different paths, followed by the same chart for every other country.

library(dplyr)

title: Greek Housing Race: Rents, House Prices and Affordability in Europe
text:
The data
The OECD serves its datasets through an SDMX API that can answer with a plain CSV, so read.csv() is all we need — no API key, no extra package. The dataset is Analytical house prices indicators (DSD_AN_HOUSE_PRICES@DF_HOUSE_PRICES). We keep the annual observations of the 29 European countries the OECD covers (EU members, Norway, Switzerland, Iceland and the United Kingdom).


Code
url <- paste0("https://sdmx.oecd.org/public/rest/data/",
              "OECD.ECO.MPD,DSD_AN_HOUSE_PRICES@DF_HOUSE_PRICES,1.0/all",
              "?startPeriod=2000&dimensionAtObservation=AllDimensions",
              "&format=csvfilewithlabels")
df_raw <- read.csv(url, fileEncoding = "UTF-8-BOM", check.names = FALSE)

df_raw$STRUCTURE_NAME<-NULL
df_raw$STRUCTURE<-NULL
df_raw$STRUCTURE_ID<-NULL
df_raw$ACTION<-NULL
df_raw$`Time period`<-NULL
df_raw$`Observation value`<-NULL
df_raw$`Base period`<-NULL
df_raw$OBS_STATUS<-NULL
df_raw$Decimals<-NULL
df_raw$DECIMALS<-NULL
df_raw$ADJUSTMENT<-NULL
df_raw$Adjustment<-NULL
df_raw$`Unit multiplier`<-NULL
df_raw$UNIT_MULT<-NULL
df_raw$OBS_STATUS<-NULL
df_raw$`Observation status`<-NULL

europe <- c("AUT", "BEL", "BGR", "HRV", "CZE", "DNK", "EST", "FIN", "FRA", "DEU",
            "GRC", "HUN", "IRL", "ITA", "LVA", "LTU", "LUX", "NLD", "POL", "PRT",
            "ROU", "SVK", "SVN", "ESP", "SWE", "NOR", "CHE", "ISL", "GBR")

df_housing <- df_raw %>%
  filter(FREQ == "A", REF_AREA %in% europe,
         MEASURE %in% c("RPI", "HPI", "HPI_YDH", "HPI_RPI")) %>%
  transmute(iso     = REF_AREA,
            country = countrycode(REF_AREA, origin = "iso3c", destination = "country.name"),
            measure = MEASURE,
            year    = as.integer(TIME_PERIOD),
            values  = round(as.numeric(OBS_VALUE), 1),
            change  = round(values - 100, 1)) %>%  # % change since 2015
  filter(!is.na(values))

Column
Description

Country name (derived from the OECD’s ISO3 REF_AREA code)

For the races we need one indicator at a time, from 2015 (where every country starts at 0%) onwards, ranked within each year, with Greece in red. A small helper does that for any of the four measures:


Code
race_data <- function(df, which, highlight = "Greece", from = 2015) {
  d <- df[df$measure == which & df$year >= from, ]
  d$rank <- ave(-d$change, d$year, FUN = function(v) rank(v, ties.method = "first"))
  d$color <- ifelse(d$country %in% highlight, "#E74C3C", "gray70")
  d
}

df_rent        <- race_data(df_housing, "RPI")      # rent prices
df_house_price <- race_data(df_housing, "HPI")      # house prices
df_income      <- race_data(df_housing, "HPI_YDH")  # house price to income
df_price_rent  <- race_data(df_housing, "HPI_RPI")  # house price to rent

title_rent        <- "How much more expensive rents got since 2015 (%)"
title_house_price <- "How much more expensive houses got since 2015 (%)"
title_price_rent  <- "How much faster house prices grew than rents since 2015 (%)"
# "+13%" / "-3%"; rounding first (+ 0 turns -0 into 0) so -0.4 reads "+0%", never "-0%"
pct <- function(v) sprintf("%+.0f%%", round(v) + 0)
title_income      <- "How much faster house prices grew than incomes since 2015 (%)"

# data source as a footnote inside each plotly chart (it stays on the chart
# when it is downloaded as a PNG from the plotly toolbar): `b` is the bottom
# margin that makes room for it; the note sits at the bottom of that margin,
# in pixels, so it lands in the same place whatever the chart's height
oecd_url <- paste0("https://data-explorer.oecd.org/vis?df[ds]=dsDisseminateFinalDMZ",
                   "&df[id]=DSD_AN_HOUSE_PRICES%40DF_HOUSE_PRICES&df[ag]=OECD.ECO.MPD")
# chart height in pixels, set on the widget itself (width stays 100% of the
# page), so the chart always fills the box it is drawn in — no scroll bars.
# Returned inside a tagList: printed straight from a chunk, a widget's height
# is overridden by the chunk's figure size; inside a tagList it is kept
# The plotly toolbar goes down the right edge, so it never covers a long title
sized <- function(p, h) {
  p <- plotly::layout(p, modebar = list(orientation = "v"))
  p$height <- h
  htmltools::tagList(p)
}

add_source <- function(p, what, b) {
  plotly::layout(p,
    margin = list(b = b),
    annotations = list(list(
      text = paste0("Source: <a href='", oecd_url, "'>OECD, Analytical house prices indicators</a>",
                    " (", what, ")"),
      xref = "paper", yref = "paper", x = 1, y = 0, yshift = -(b - 22),
      xanchor = "right", yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE,
      font = list(size = 11, color = "gray50"))))
}

                                x = 0.02, xanchor = "left",

text:
Building the visualisations

Step 1 — bar chart race, ranked
The frame argument of plot_ly turns a bar chart into a play/pause animation stepping through each year, and plotting by rank instead of country name makes the bars physically reorder every year. Greece is layered on top in red so it is always visible against the gray field. The same function draws four races: rents, house prices, and house prices relative to incomes and to rents.


Code
bar_race <- function(d, title, what) {
  plot_ly() %>%
    add_bars(data = d[d$color == "gray70", ],
             x = ~rank, y = ~change, frame = ~year, ids = ~rank,
             marker = list(color = "gray70"),
             text = ~paste0(country, " ", sprintf("%+.0f%%", change)), hoverinfo = "text",
             textposition = "outside", textangle = 90, showlegend = FALSE) %>%
    add_bars(data = d[d$color %in% "#E74C3C", ],
             x = ~rank, y = ~change, frame = ~year, ids = ~rank,
             marker = list(color = "#E74C3C"),
             text = ~paste0(country, " ", sprintf("%+.0f%%", change)), hoverinfo = "text",
             textposition = "outside", textangle = 90, showlegend = FALSE) %>%
    layout(xaxis  = list(title = "Rank", tickmode = "array"),
           yaxis  = list(title = "% vs 2015", ticksuffix = "%"),
           title  = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
           margin = list(l = 50, r = 30, t = 70),
           font   = list(size = 13, color = "gray25")) %>%
    animation_opts(frame = 1000, transition = 0, easing = "linear", redraw = TRUE) %>%
    add_source(what, b = 200) %>%
    sized(620)
}

bar_race(df_rent, title_rent, "rent prices, RPI")






Code

Code

race_gif <- function(d, title, file) {
  n_countries <- max(d$rank)
  hi  <- max(d$change)
  lo  <- min(0, min(d$change))   # a few markets were below 2015 for a while
  pad <- (hi - lo) * 0.02

  p <- ggplot(d, aes(x = rank, y = change, fill = color, group = country)) +
    geom_col(width = 0.85, show.legend = FALSE) +
    # country names left of the panel, value at the end of each bar
    geom_text(aes(y = lo - pad, label = country, color = color),
              hjust = 1, size = 3.8, fontface = "bold", show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_text(aes(y = pmax(change, 0) + pad, label = pct(change)),
              hjust = 0, color = "gray80", size = 3.2) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "#546E7A", linewidth = 0.4) +
    scale_fill_identity() +
    scale_color_identity() +
    scale_x_reverse(breaks = NULL) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = function(v) paste0(v, "%"),
                       expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.1))) +
    geom_text(
      data = d %>% dplyr::distinct(year),
      aes(x = n_countries, y = hi, label = year),
      inherit.aes = FALSE,
      hjust = 1, vjust = 0,
      size = 20, color = "white", alpha = 0.15,
      fontface = "bold"
    ) +
    coord_flip(clip = "off") +
    labs(title   = title,
         x       = NULL,
         y       = "% vs 2015",
         caption = "Source: OECD Analytical house prices indicators  |  Greece highlighted in red") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(
      plot.background    = element_rect(fill = "#0F1923", color = NA),
      panel.background   = element_rect(fill = "#0F1923", color = NA),
      panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "#1E2D3D", linewidth = 0.4),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
      axis.text.x   = element_text(color = "#90A4AE", size = 10),
      axis.text.y   = element_blank(),
      axis.title.x  = element_text(color = "#90A4AE", size = 10),
      plot.title    = element_text(color = "white", face = "bold", size = 12,
                                    margin = margin(12, 0, 8, 0)),
      plot.caption  = element_text(color = "#546E7A", size = 8, hjust = 1,
                                    margin = margin(8, 0, 8, 0)),
      plot.margin   = margin(10, 40, 10, 130)) +
    transition_states(year, transition_length = 0, state_length = 5) +
    ease_aes("cubic-in-out")

  animate(p,
          nframes  = 100,
          fps      = 10,
          duration = 20,
          width    = 900,
          height   = 900,
          units    = "px",
          res      = 100,   # set explicitly: when knitting, gganimate otherwise uses the chunk dpi
          renderer = gifski_renderer(file))
}

title: Greek Housing Race: Rents, House Prices and Affordability in Europe
text:
What the charts show

In Greece, rents kept falling after 2015 and bottomed out in 2018 (-8% against 2015). By 2025 they were +13%, while house prices were +79%: since 2015, buying has become far more expensive than renting.
House prices also outran incomes: the price-to-income ratio was +18% against 2015, which puts Greece 9th of 28 European countries in how much less affordable homes have become.
In the house price race Greece was 16th of 29, and in the price-to-rent race 9th of 27 (+58%): since 2015, house prices in Greece have outgrown rents by that much.
In the rent race Greece was 25th of 27 in 2025: rents rose less there than in most of Europe. The race ranks how much each market moved since 2015, not which country has the most expensive rents.
A caveat for Greece: the OECD rent index comes from the rents in consumer price statistics, which follow all tenancies, most of them on older contracts. Rents asked for new leases, the ones a person moving house actually faces, have risen much faster than this index shows — listing-based indices (e.g. Spitogatos or the Bank of Greece’s analyses) are the place to look for those.

text:
Part 2 — Maps (overview)

How the shapefiles work
NSIDC also publishes the sea ice boundary as a polygon shapefile for every month. We download and cache them locally, then read with sf.


Code
month_dirs <- c("01_Jan","02_Feb","03_Mar","04_Apr","05_May","06_Jun",
                "07_Jul","08_Aug","09_Sep","10_Oct","11_Nov","12_Dec")

fetch_ice_extent <- function(year, month = "09", pole = "N",
                             tmpdir = file.path(tempdir(), "nsidc_ice")) {
  dir.create(tmpdir, showWarnings = FALSE)
  mm       <- sprintf("%02d", as.integer(month))
  yymm     <- paste0(year, mm)
  pole_dir <- ifelse(pole == "N", "north", "south")
  mon_dir  <- month_dirs[as.integer(mm)]
  url <- paste0(
    "https://noaadata.apps.nsidc.org/NOAA/G02135/",
    pole_dir, "/monthly/shapefiles/shp_extent/", mon_dir, "/",
    "extent_", pole, "_", yymm, "_polygon_v4.0.zip"
  )
  zip_path <- file.path(tmpdir, paste0("ice_", pole, "_", yymm, ".zip"))
  if (!file.exists(zip_path) || file.size(zip_path) < 1000) {
    message("Downloading ", year, "-", mm, " ...")
    tryCatch(
      download.file(url, zip_path, quiet = TRUE, mode = "wb"),
      error = function(e) { message("  failed: ", e$message); return(NULL) }
    )
  }
  if (!file.exists(zip_path) || file.size(zip_path) < 1000) return(NULL)
  exdir <- file.path(tmpdir, paste0("ice_", pole, "_", yymm))
  suppressWarnings(unzip(zip_path, exdir = exdir, overwrite = FALSE))
  shp <- list.files(exdir, "\\.shp$", full.names = TRUE)[1]
  if (is.na(shp)) return(NULL)
  shape <- tryCatch(sf::st_read(shp, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(shape)) return(NULL)
  shape$year <- year
  shape
}

text:
Packages


Code

#                     "eurostat", "gganimate", "gifski", "scales", "ragg"))

library(dplyr)

title: EU Salary Race: Average Full-Time Adjusted Wages
text:
The data
get_eurostat() downloads the raw dataset table by its Eurostat code. We keep only country-level rows (dropping the EU27_2020 and EA20 aggregates), derive a plain-language country name and ISO code with countrycode, and rank countries by salary within each year.


Code
df_eusalary <- get_eurostat("nama_10_fte", filters = list(unit = "EUR"))
df_eusalary <- df_eusalary[!df_eusalary$geo %in% c("EU27_2020", "EA20"), ]

df_eusalary$year    <- lubridate::year(df_eusalary$time)
df_eusalary$country <- countrycode(df_eusalary$geo, origin = "eurostat", destination = "country.name")
df_eusalary$iso     <- countrycode(df_eusalary$geo, origin = "eurostat", destination = "iso2c")

df_eusalary$rank  <- NA
df_eusalary$color <- NA
for (i in unique(df_eusalary$year)) {
  df_eusalary[df_eusalary$year %in% i, "rank"] <-
    rank(-df_eusalary[df_eusalary$year %in% i, "values"], ties.method = "min")
}

df_eusalary[df_eusalary$country %in% "Greece", "color"]  <- "#E74C3C"
df_eusalary[!df_eusalary$country %in% "Greece", "color"] <- "gray70"

text:
Building the visualisations

Step 1 — interactive time series
A line per country lets you trace how each economy moved over time, and hovering reveals the exact value.


Code
colors <- c("#e6194b", "#3cb44b", "#ffe119", "#0082c8", "#f58231", "#911eb4", "#46f0f0",
            "#f032e6", "#d2f53c", "#fabebe", "#008080", "#e6beff", "#aa6e28", "#fffac8",
            "#800000", "#aaffc3", "#808000", "#ffd8b1", "#000080", "#808080", "#ffffff",
            "#000000")

plot_ly(df_eusalary[df_eusalary$values > 0, ],
        x = ~year,
        y = ~values,
        color = ~country,
        mode = "lines+markers",
        type = "scatter",
        text = ~paste("Year:", year,
                      "<br>Value:", values,
                      "<br>Country Name:", country),
        hoverinfo = "text",
        colors = colors,
        showlegend = TRUE,
        marker = list(size = 8)) %>%
  plotly::layout(title = "",
                 autosize = TRUE,
                 margin = list(l = 50, r = 50, b = 50, t = 50, pad = 0),
                 legend = list(orientation = "vertical", xanchor = "right", x = 30, y = 1),
                 xaxis = list(title = "Year", tickangle = -90),
                 yaxis = list(title = ""),
                 font = list(size = 20, color = "gray25", weight = "bold"))








Step 2 — animated bar chart
Sliding a frame argument to plot_ly turns a static bar chart into a play/pause animation stepping through each year.


Code
plot_ly(df_eusalary,
        x = ~country,
        y = ~values,
        frame = ~year,
        ids = ~country,
        type = "bar",
        text = ~paste("Year:", year,
                      "<br>Value:", values,
                      "<br>Country:", country),
        hoverinfo = "text",
        colors = colors,
        showlegend = FALSE) %>%
  layout(
    title  = title,
    xaxis  = list(title = "", tickangle = -90),
    yaxis  = list(title = "Euro"),
    font   = list(size = 20, color = "gray25", weight = "bold"),
    margin = list(l = 50, r = 50, b = 200, t = 100)
  ) %>%
  animation_opts(
    frame = 500,
    transition = 500,
    easing = "linear",
    redraw = FALSE,
    mode = "immediate"
  )








Step 3 — bar chart race, ranked
Instead of plotting by country name, we plot by rank, so the bars physically reorder every year as economies overtake each other. Greece is layered on top in red so it’s always visible against the gray field.


Code
plot_ly() %>%
  add_bars(
    data         = df_eusalary[df_eusalary$color == "gray70", ],
    x            = ~rank,
    y            = ~values,
    frame        = ~year,
    ids          = ~rank,
    marker       = list(color = "gray70"),
    text         = ~country,
    hoverinfo    = "text",
    textposition = "outside",
    textangle    = 90,
    showlegend   = FALSE
  ) %>%
  add_bars(
    data         = df_eusalary[df_eusalary$color %in% "#E74C3C", ],
    x            = ~rank,
    y            = ~values,
    frame        = ~year,
    ids          = ~rank,
    marker       = list(color = "#E74C3C"),
    text         = ~country,
    hoverinfo    = "text",
    textposition = "outside",
    textangle    = 90,
    showlegend   = FALSE
  ) %>%
  layout(
    xaxis  = list(title = "Rank", tickmode = "array"),
    yaxis  = list(title = "Euro"),
    title  = title,
    margin = list(l = 50, r = 50, b = 200, t = 100),
    font   = list(size = 20, color = "gray25", weight = "bold")
  ) %>%
  animation_opts(frame = 1000, transition = 0, easing = "linear", redraw = TRUE)








Step 4 — dark themed GIF with gganimate
The interactive versions above are great for exploring in a browser, but a rendered GIF is easier to share. ggplot2 + gganimate recreates the same ranked race as a horizontal bar chart with a dark background, country labels, and a large year watermark.


Code
p <- ggplot(df_eusalary, aes(x = rank, y = values, fill = color, group = country)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.85, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(y = 0, label = country, color = color),
            hjust = 1, nudge_y = -400,
            size = 3.8, fontface = "bold", show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = comma(values, accuracy = 1)),
            hjust = 0, nudge_y = 400,
            color = "gray80", size = 3.2) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  scale_color_identity() +
  scale_x_reverse(breaks = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = comma,
    breaks = seq(0, 100000, by = 20000),
    limits = c(-8000, NA),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.08))
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = df_eusalary %>% dplyr::distinct(year),
    aes(x = 23, y = 85000, label = year),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    hjust = 1, vjust = 1,
    size = 20, color = "white", alpha = 0.15,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  coord_flip(clip = "off") +
  labs(title   = title,
       x       = NULL,
       y       = "Euros",
       caption = "Source: Eurostat  |  Greece highlighted in red") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    plot.background    = element_rect(fill = "#0F1923", color = NA),
    panel.background   = element_rect(fill = "#0F1923", color = NA),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "#1E2D3D", linewidth = 0.4),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor.x = element_line(color = "#1E2D3D", linewidth = 0.4),
    axis.text.x   = element_text(color = "#90A4AE", size = 10),
    axis.text.y   = element_blank(),
    plot.title    = element_text(color = "white", face = "bold", size = 10,
                                  margin = margin(12, 0, 2, 0)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "gray80", face = "bold", size = 10,
                                  hjust = 0.98,
                                  margin = margin(0, 0, 6, 0)),
    plot.caption  = element_text(color = "#546E7A", size = 8, hjust = 1,
                                  margin = margin(8, 0, 8, 0)),
    plot.margin   = margin(10, 30, 10, 120)) +
  transition_states(year, transition_length = 0, state_length = 5) +
  ease_aes("cubic-in-out")

animate(p,
        nframes  = 100,
        fps      = 10,
        duration = 20,
        width    = 900,
        height   = 800,
        units    = "px",
        res      = 100,   # set explicitly: when knitting, gganimate otherwise uses the chunk dpi (300 x retina 2)
        renderer = gifski_renderer(paste0(directory,"eu_salary_race.gif")))

title: EU Salary Race: Average Full-Time Adjusted Wages
text:
What the chart shows

Northern and Western European economies (e.g. Denmark, Luxembourg, Ireland) consistently occupy the top ranks across the whole period.
Greece sits in the lower half of the ranking throughout, and its relative position (highlighted in red) makes the post-2010 economic crisis visible as a plateau while other countries continue climbing.
Ranks shuffle more among mid-table countries than at the extremes — the top and bottom of the distribution are comparatively stable year to year.
